Phase 04 · 8–11 hours

Slab & geometry.

A slab remembers rolling, bending, support, and drying. Learn to manage the sheet before asking it to become architecture.

Run the variables labSee the folded vessel

Aim

Make the plane behave.

Prerequisite

Moisture-state judgment, controlled compression, and secure joins from Phases 1–3.

By the end

Prepare stable slabs, choose a joining state, build crisp or soft geometry, and diagnose warp from process evidence.

Deliverables

Six variable tiles, seam coupons, a lidded box, a dart/mold study, and one folded vessel.

04.1

A slab is a stressed sheet.

Why can a perfectly flat slab curve later—even when nobody touches it?

Four variables

Thickness · compression · moisture · constraint

Rolling stretches and orients a sheet. Turning, compressing both faces, equalizing moisture, and controlling support reduce—not eliminate—the stresses that reappear in drying and firing.

Evidence over recipes

Thickness and waiting times depend on clay, scale, support, and intended use. Use edge firmness, flex, surface sheen, and response to lifting to decide when to cut or join.

Lab · Six-tile variables matrix90 min + drying

Roll six equal tiles. Change one condition per pair: one-direction versus rotated rolling; one-face versus two-face compression; exposed versus evenly covered drying. Mark the underside.

  1. Measure corner lift and diagonal twist at leather hard and bone dry.
  2. Photograph every tile from the same low angle.
  3. State what the comparison supports—and what it cannot prove from six samples.
04.2

Design the seam before joining it.

Lab · Seam coupons75–90 min

Build pairs of small L-shaped samples using butt, bevel, and supported interior joins. Keep slab state and dimensions consistent.

  1. Score only enough to texture the contact; use slip as needed for your clay and state.
  2. Compress across the boundary without thinning the corner.
  3. At firm leather hard, section one of each pair. Dry the others and record crack location.
Important:“Score and slip” is not a universal spell. Moisture compatibility, intimate contact, compression, geometry, support, and drying determine whether a joint survives.

Guided build · Lidded box

  1. Make a paper maquette first; resolve panel order and lid overlap.
  2. Cut slabs only when they can lift without stretching yet still accept compression.
  3. Join opposing walls in sequence to distribute stress. Check diagonals for squareness.
  4. Fit the lid at the same moisture state and design tolerance for shrinkage and glaze thickness.
04.3

Turn plane into volume.

Dart

Remove a wedge and close the gap. The flat sheet becomes compound volume.

Drape

Let gravity and a form create a soft transition. Separate with appropriate material and remove support before shrinkage locks it.

Fold

Compress a controlled hinge rather than sharply creasing a dry or over-thin sheet.

Study · One template, three volumes2 hours

Use the same paper outline to make a darted form, a draped form, and a folded form. Record how each method changes interior volume, edge behavior, and drying risk.

SymptomInspectTargeted response
Corner liftsCompression, drying exposure, base constraintRun a paired tile test; equalize drying.
Join opensClay states and contact lineRepeat coupon with matched moisture and better support.
Panel bowsSlab softness and handling stretchJoin later or add temporary non-sticking support.
04.4

Project: folded envelope vessel.

Integrated project

One sheet, a convincing volume.

Design an 18–25 cm vessel from a single dominant slab with folds, darts, or one closing seam. Let planar logic remain visible.

  1. Make three paper maquettes and test stability, access, and visual direction.
  2. Select one. Mark compression direction, fold lines, seam order, and supported zones on the template.
  3. Build and document clay-state cues at rolling, cutting, lifting, joining, and support removal.
  4. Dry on an absorbent, movable board with exposure adjusted to equalize—not accelerate—drying.
  5. Evaluate silhouette, seam integrity, planar clarity, base stability, and warp evidence.

Inspiration · look comparatively

Geometry can be faceted, wrapped, or pressed into relief.

Use these as studies of planes becoming volume. Only the mask vessel has a cataloged modeled-clay-sheet construction; the others are formal comparisons.

Knowledge check · 3 questions

Pause. Predict. Diagnose.

Choose one answer for each situation. Open a hint when needed; explanations appear after you check all three.
